column3: It closely repeats the demand that an angel be sent down to the messenger and answers it by showing that such a descent would end the period of reprieve.
Its reward for what believers said shares only a generic verb of speech and does not address the messenger, food, markets, or an angel.
It affirms that the addressee is one of the messengers, but does not engage the objection to his ordinary human life.
It directly answers the charge: every earlier messenger ate food and walked in markets, and this shared human setting is part of the test between people.
The immediate response calls their descriptions of the messenger false analogies and shows that their objections have led them away from the path.
The sending of devils against disbelievers does not clarify the requested angel or the human messenger's life.
It presents a related status-based objection to revelation: opponents demand that it descend upon a socially great man rather than accept its actual bearer.
It continues the same catalogue of demands for wealth and a garden, then records the opponents' charge that the messenger is bewitched.
Noah's declaration that he is a clear warner gives the messenger's role, but not the objection to a human warner.
It closely parallels the demand for a treasure or an accompanying angel and explicitly replies that the messenger is only a warner.
The preceding verse identifies the revelation's source in the One who knows secrets, supplying the response context for the opponents' demand in the focus.
It joins the truthful descent of the Quran with the messenger's role as bearer of good news and warning, rather than an angelic display.
It explicitly says earlier messengers were not bodies exempt from eating food or death, directly normalizing the humanity attacked in the focus.
God's knowledge of open and hidden speech does not materially address the claim about a messenger eating and walking in markets.
It identifies the message as a warner continuous with earlier warnings, but does not address the desired angelic companion.
It parallels the demand for additional signs and answers that signs belong to God while the prophet's assigned role is clear warning.
This judgment dialogue about false objects of worship does not illuminate the opponents' objection to the messenger.
It names the Quran a merciful and mighty revelation, but does not connect that descent to the requested angel or human messenger.
It calls Christ a messenger and notes that he and his mother ate food, a direct rebuttal to treating ordinary bodily need as disqualifying.
It continues the response to demands for wealth by affirming that God could grant gardens and palaces, so their demand does not measure prophetic truth.
Its command to walk the earth and eat provision concerns human life generally, not a messenger's alleged unfitness.
It repeats the unbelievers' demand for a sign to be sent down to the prophet and redirects the issue to God's guidance rather than spectacle.
It establishes the Quran as the criterion sent down upon God's servant so that he may warn all worlds, framing the actual basis of his mission.
Walking through the dwellings of destroyed peoples is unrelated to the messenger walking in markets.
Feeding the needy is ethically significant but does not bear on the focus's objection to prophetic humanity.
God's knowledge of what people conceal and disclose offers no specific support for the angel or messenger issue.
It confirms that warners were sent among earlier peoples, but adds no detail about their humanity or accompanying signs.
Its affirmation of angels, books, and messengers supplies broad belief context but does not address an angel being demanded as a co-warner.
Its contrast between a promised eternal garden and the opponents' preference is local context, but it does not directly clarify their demand in 25:7.
The leaders' command to persist with their gods uses walking figuratively and concerns a different dispute.
It states that God could have sent a separate warner to every town, making the requested additional warner a question of divine choice rather than necessity.
The next movement exposes denial of the Hour as the deeper issue behind the opponents' escalating demands.
The rejection of Aad and its warning supplies a broad precedent for refusing a warner, without the focus's human-or-angel question.
The record of deeds at judgment does not clarify the nature or credentials of the messenger.
The earlier granting of the Criterion to Moses and Aaron offers a broad precedent for divinely given guidance, not the focus's objection.
The sending of the she-camel as a test is a different kind of sign and does not explain the role of a human messenger.
Food and the Torah occur in a legal challenge, not in a discussion of prophetic humanity or an angelic companion.
The local regret at not taking a path with the messenger shows the eventual cost of dismissing the one mocked in the focus.
It explicitly states that God sent down the Quran to the prophet, providing the actual mode of divine communication instead of the demanded angelic accompaniment.
It closely reproduces the objection: a messenger is dismissed as merely human because he eats and drinks as his people do.
This local taunt portrays the opponents as resisting the messenger because they think he threatens their gods, clarifying the motive behind their mockery.
The descent of rain and the growth of plants do not bear on the descent of an angel to accompany a messenger.
It describes a warning to humankind, but is too general to clarify who bears that warning or why an angel is demanded.
The measured descent of created things is not about revelation, a messenger, or the requested angel.
It defines the prophet's sending as mercy to all worlds, positively framing the mission the opponents reduce to worldly expectations.
Wealth and sons appear as a trait of a rejecter, without a meaningful connection to the focus.
Its judgment on those driven face-down to Hell is local consequence context, but it does not explain the objection in 25:7.
The repeated question about punishment and warnings offers a general consequence for rejecting warnings, not the focus's specific demand.
The messenger and believers striving together does not illuminate the objection to his ordinary life.
It directly records the opponents' ridicule: they mock the very person whom God sent as a messenger.
It gives a generic warning of blazing fire without addressing the bearer of warning or the request for an angel.
God's creative command does not clarify prophetic warning or the opponents' proposed sign.
God's knowledge of secret conversations is not materially related to the focus's objection.
Earlier messengers brought clear proofs and their rejecters were punished, a broad precedent with no human-or-angel issue.
The divine command that brings things into being is unrelated to the messenger's public life and role.
The local diagnosis that most of them neither hear nor reason explains why the stated objections fail to engage the message itself.
Hud's warning and the succession of prior warners provide a general prophetic precedent, but not the focus's requested angel.
It details the messenger's ethical and revelatory mission and the light sent down with him, supplying a substantive alternative to the opponents' demand for display.
The description of the Fire's confinement is later judgment context and does not clarify the focus's dispute.
It identifies the Quran as a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, but does not engage the demand for an angelic companion.
God's sole possession of intercession is unrelated to the messenger's food, markets, or warning role.
Salih brings a clear sign and commands respect for it, but the reference does not directly address whether a messenger must be angelic.
It reports the sending of multiple messengers, yet does not state the objection to their humanity found in the focus.
The command to honor an orphan's property and fulfill covenants is unrelated to the focus.
The local statement that the messenger seeks no payment and only invites people toward their Lord clarifies the purpose of the mission under attack.
The command to arise and warn concisely states the prophetic function for which the opponents demand an unnecessary angelic duplicate.
Jesus is sent as a messenger with signs by God's permission, showing that signs serve a mission but do not make prophetic authority self-owned.
The command to call for much destruction in Hell does not bear on the claim about the messenger.
It limits the messenger's task to warning those who fear the Hour, directly clarifying the warning function at issue in the focus.
Creation, resurrection, and God's knowledge do not specifically illuminate the opponents' demand for an angel.
Thamud challenge Salih to bring the punishment he promises while acknowledging his messenger status, a general pattern of defiant rejection.
It identifies the book sent down to the prophet as the means by which he warns people, directly grounding his mission in revelation rather than an angelic companion.
The required response to slander is unrelated to the focus's dispute over the messenger.
Walking humbly on earth describes God's servants generally, not the messenger's market-going life or the demand for an angel.
It simply identifies Elijah as a messenger and offers no interpretive detail for the focus.
The believers' trial and expectation of divine help do not concern the messenger's humanity or warning role.
It directly defines the addressee's commission as bearer of good news and warning, answering the claimed need for an angel to warn alongside him.
It states the same basic objection in general form: people reject messengers because they are human beings who would guide them.
God's creative decree has no material relation to the requested angel or public prophetic life.
It calls the Quran a blessed reminder sent down and challenges its rejection, shifting attention from demanded spectacle to the revelation already given.
The parable of intermittent light and darkness does not address a messenger or angelic validation.
Its reference to people and animals eating belongs to a parable of worldly life, not the objection to a food-eating messenger.
The local regret of being diverted from the reminder after it came shows the consequence of letting hostile influence displace the messenger's message.
It names the Quran as a revelation from the Creator, but does not address the opponents' criteria for a messenger.
It identifies Muhammad as God's messenger, but does not engage the human-versus-angel objection.
The description of the Garden's food and shade has no interpretive connection to the focus.
It presents the prophet's mission as mercy and warning to a people without a prior warner, supporting the sufficiency of his assigned role.
The women's contrast between Joseph's human appearance and an angel provides a relevant human-versus-angel distinction, though outside a prophetic dispute.
The destroyed people's final cry does not address the nature or mission of a messenger.
It merely identifies Lot as a messenger, with no direct relation to the focus's objection.
The account of hypocrites' disbelief and resentment does not illuminate the requested angel or a messenger's ordinary life.
It identifies Gabriel as the one who brought the Quran to the prophet's heart by God's permission, distinguishing revelation's angelic mediation from the demanded public co-warner.
Aad's arrogant denial of God's signs reflects the rejecting disposition behind such demands, but not their specific form.
The prophet is commanded to recite the Quran and say that he is only among the warners, closely defining the task challenged in the focus.
The prophet's movement among worshippers does not clarify the opponents' demand for an angel or objection to market-going.
It states that no town is destroyed without warners, affirming the sufficiency and seriousness of the warning function.
It recalls earlier peoples who received clear proofs from their messengers, a broad historical background for rejecting prophetic guidance.
The description of a habitual slanderer does not bear on the focus.
God's ownership and self-sufficiency do not specifically clarify the messenger or the desired angel.
Its metaphor of a person walking among people by divine light does not materially address the human messenger or angelic accompaniment.
It records the demand that God speak directly or provide a sign, a broader form of the insistence on visible validation behind 25:7.
The question whether they await God and the angels to come openly parallels the opponents' demand for an overwhelming visible divine intervention.
Israel's demand to see God openly supplies a related precedent for escalating evidentiary demands beyond the message already given.
It addresses the wish for a sign from heaven and places such signs under God's will, not the messenger's control.
It directly reports the demand that a sign be sent down to the prophet and replies that God is able to send one, though most do not understand.
The prophet disavows possessing divine treasuries, unseen knowledge, or angelic status, directly clarifying the limits opponents mistake for disqualification.
It warns that even sworn demands for signs do not guarantee belief, exposing the inadequacy of treating spectacle as the missing condition.
It states that even if angels descended and the dead spoke, the rejecters would still not believe unless God willed, directly answering the premise of the angel demand.
It addresses human descendants through messengers from among themselves who recite God's signs, affirming ordinary human mediation of warning.
It identifies the opponents' amazement that revelation came to a man from among them, closely matching their resistance to a human messenger.
It repeats the demand for a sign from the messenger's Lord and redirects the issue to God's unseen governance and patient waiting.
Noah's chiefs dismiss him as only a human like themselves and disparage his followers, a close historical parallel to the focus's social objection.
Noah denies claiming divine treasuries, unseen knowledge, or being an angel, directly distinguishing prophetic office from the status opponents demand.
It states that those sent before were men from towns to whom revelation came, directly establishing the human character of messengers.
The unbelievers again ask why a sign was not sent down upon the prophet, while the verse defines him as a warner and assigns guidance to God.
It says no messenger can bring a sign except by God's permission, limiting the demand for a sign or angel to divine decision.
The messengers acknowledge that they are humans like their peoples, while grounding their distinction in God's favor and revelation rather than angelic nature.
The opponents call the recipient of the revelation mad, an accusation that helps locate the contempt driving their demand for another kind of messenger.
They demand that he bring angels if he is truthful, a direct parallel to the requested angel in 25:7.
It answers that angels are not sent down except with the decisive truth, after which rejecters receive no reprieve.
It recalls that messengers before the prophet were also sent among earlier factions, giving a broad precedent for his contested mission.
It describes God sending angels with the Spirit and revelation by His command, distinguishing real angelic descent from opponents' chosen validation test.
It explicitly states that God sent only men to whom He revealed, directly rejecting the assumption that a messenger must be angelic.
The demand for a spring from the earth is a close parallel to the material proofs opponents require instead of receiving the messenger's warning.
The demand for a garden with rivers closely parallels the wealth-and-garden expectation that continues immediately after 25:7.
It directly demands that the prophet bring God and the angels face to face, intensifying the same appeal for visible angelic confirmation.
The demand for ascent to heaven and a readable book extends the pattern of refusing the revelation and messenger already present.
It identifies the central impediment to belief as surprise that God sent a human being as messenger, directly naming the focus's objection.
It explains that an angelic messenger would be appropriate only if angels lived securely on earth; human inhabitants receive a human messenger.
The prophet declares that he is a human like his audience who receives revelation, directly joining human likeness with the true mark of his office.
The angels say they descend only by their Lord's command, offering a limited corrective to the assumption that they appear on human demand.
The opponents ask why the prophet has not brought a sign from his Lord, a direct parallel to their demand for further validation.
The wrongdoers dismiss the prophet as a human like themselves and call the revelation magic, closely matching the focus's contemptuous logic.
Their shifting accusations culminate in demanding a sign like those sent with earlier messengers, showing the same refusal to receive the present revelation.
It reiterates that God sent only men to whom He revealed, directly answering the human-versus-angel premise.
A people's leaders reject their prophet as merely human like them and say God would have sent angels if He willed, an exceptionally close parallel.
They argue that obeying a human who eats and drinks as they do would mean loss, directly echoing the food-based objection in 25:7.
Pharaoh's people refuse to believe in two humans like themselves, providing another direct case of rejecting human prophetic mediators.
The local accusation that the Quran was fabricated shows that the objection to the messenger is bound to rejection of the revelation he bears.
The charge that the Quran consists of dictated ancient tales continues the local effort to discredit the message rather than hear its warning.
The opponents ask why angels were not sent down to them or why they cannot see their Lord, directly repeating the demand for visible heavenly confirmation.
It reverses the desired angelic appearance by stating that seeing angels will bring no good news to criminals, not the validation they seek.
The objection that the Quran was not sent down all at once receives a direct explanation that its measured descent strengthens the prophet's heart.
God answers that whenever opponents bring a false analogy, He supplies the truth and the best explanation, directly interpreting the rhetoric of 25:7-9.
Salih is dismissed as only a human like his people and challenged to bring a sign, combining both objections central to the focus.
Shuayb is rejected as only a human like his people and accused of lying, another direct historical parallel to contempt for a human messenger.
The demand that fragments of heaven fall if the prophet is truthful illustrates the same escalation toward spectacular proof.
When truth reaches them, opponents demand an earlier-style sign like Moses received, showing that the present revelation is rejected through comparative demands.
The prophet's lack of prior reading or writing supports the integrity of the revelation that opponents try to discredit through alternative explanations.
It asks whether the revealed book recited to them is not sufficient, directly challenging the premise that another sign or angel is required.
Opponents call the prophet merely a man seeking to turn them from ancestral worship and call the Quran fabricated, closely paralleling the focus's dismissal.
Those addressed reject the messengers as only humans like themselves and deny that the Merciful sent anything down, directly matching both human and revelation objections.
The disbelievers marvel that a warner has come from among them, directly paralleling the astonishment at a human messenger.
They object that the reminder was sent down specifically to him, a status-based form of the same refusal to accept God's chosen messenger.
It states that messengers cannot bring signs except by God's permission, again denying that opponents may dictate the required proof.
The prophet is commanded to say that he is a human like his audience who receives revelation, directly defining the distinction missed in 25:7.
When messengers call people to worship God, they answer that God would have sent angels if He wished, a direct parallel to the focus's angel demand.
Pharaoh asks why Moses lacks material adornment and why angels do not accompany him, an especially close precedent for demanding angelic accompaniment and worldly status.
The prophet says he is not unprecedented among messengers, follows only revelation, and is only a clear warner, directly clarifying the office questioned in the focus.
The disbelievers are amazed that a warner came from among them, directly reflecting their resistance to an ordinary human bearer of warning.
Thamud ask whether they should follow a single human from among themselves, a close historical instance of the same objection.
They protest that the reminder was sent down upon him in particular, continuing the challenge to God's choice of a human messenger.
The prophet limits his knowledge of the Hour and identifies himself as a clear warner, clarifying that warning does not entail control of unseen proof or timing.
